questions.text: What does the PATH variable normally influence in a Linux shell?
options: Which command locations the shell searches for executable names
questions.correctAnswer: Which command locations the shell searches for executable names
questions.explanation:
PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched when running a command by name.

Why: The shell searches those paths for a matching executable.

Example: echo "$PATH" displays the search list.

Student note: A program outside PATH can still be run by using its path.

study.title: PATH variable
study.simple: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched when running a command by name.
steps: The shell searches those paths for a matching executable.
study.example: echo "$PATH" displays the search list.
study.pitfall: A program outside PATH can still be run by using its path.
study.remember: The shell searches those paths for a matching executable.

keyTerms.meaning: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched when running a command by name.

questions.text: Which command changes the prompt for the current Bash session?
questions.explanation:
PS1 controls the primary Bash prompt's displayed text.

Why: Assigning PS1 in the current shell changes the prompt for that session.

Example: PS1='ict2631> ' displays a simple custom prompt.

Student note: Make a change persistent via the appropriate shell startup file, not a random system file.

study.remember: Assigning PS1 in the current shell changes the prompt for that session.

keyTerms.meaning: PS1 controls the primary Bash prompt's displayed text.

questions.text: Why does echo '$HOME' normally print the literal characters $HOME?
options: Single quotes stop normal shell variable expansion
questions.correctAnswer: Single quotes stop normal shell variable expansion
questions.explanation:
Single quotes preserve the literal contents, while double quotes still allow variable expansion.

Why: The shell sees the dollar sign as text inside single quotes.

Example: echo "$HOME" usually prints the home-directory path.

Student note: Expansion is performed by the shell before echo receives its arguments.

steps: The shell sees the dollar sign as text inside single quotes.
study.example: echo "$HOME" usually prints the home-directory path.
study.pitfall: Expansion is performed by the shell before echo receives its arguments.
study.remember: The shell sees the dollar sign as text inside single quotes.

keyTerms.meaning: Single quotes preserve the literal contents, while double quotes still allow variable expansion.

questions.text: What is the effect of >> when writing command output to an existing file?
questions.explanation:
The shell redirects standard output with > or >>.

Why: >> appends; > normally overwrites the destination file.

Example: date >> journal.txt adds a line without replacing earlier content.

Student note: Check a destination before using >, especially for an important log.

study.remember: >> appends; > normally overwrites the destination file.

keyTerms.meaning: The shell redirects standard output with > or >>.

questions.text: Which operator passes standard output of one command as standard input to another?
questions.explanation:
A pipe connects the output stream of one command to the input stream of another.

Why: It enables small tools to work together.

Example: ps aux | grep ssh searches process listings for ssh.

Student note: A pipe is not the same as writing output into a named file.

questions.text: You want all regular files under /home/student with a .txt suffix. Which command fits?
questions.explanation:
find traverses paths and filters entries by properties such as type and name.

Why: -type f selects regular files, and -name uses a pattern.

Example: Quoting '*.txt' prevents the current shell expanding it too soon.

Student note: find works on filesystem entries, whereas grep searches content.

questions.text: Which command shows running processes with user and command information?
questions.explanation:

Why: The aux format is widely used for a detailed process listing.

Example: ps aux | grep nginx searches for matching process text.

Student note: top or htop is more useful for a continuously changing view.

questions.text: What is a sensible first signal for asking an ordinary process to exit cleanly?
questions.explanation:
Signals ask a process to take an action; TERM normally requests termination.

Why: An application may use TERM to finish work and release resources.

Example: kill -TERM 1234 requests a clean stop of process 1234.

Student note: SIGKILL cannot be caught, so reserve it for cases where gentler actions fail.

questions.text: What does a positive nice value normally mean for a Linux process?
options: Lower CPU scheduling priority than a process with a smaller nice value
questions.correctAnswer: Lower CPU scheduling priority than a process with a smaller nice value
questions.explanation:
Niceness adjusts normal scheduling priority; larger nice values usually mean a process is more willing to yield CPU time.

Why: It helps control resource contention.

Example: nice -n 10 long-task starts a task with a higher niceness value.

Student note: Niceness is not a hard CPU percentage limit.

study.simple: Niceness adjusts normal scheduling priority; larger nice values usually mean a process is more willing to yield CPU time.
steps: It helps control resource contention.

study.pitfall: Niceness is not a hard CPU percentage limit.
study.remember: It helps control resource contention.

keyTerms.meaning: Niceness adjusts normal scheduling priority; larger nice values usually mean a process is more willing to yield CPU time.

questions.text: Why might a machine use swap space?
options: To extend virtual-memory backing when RAM pressure occurs, at a performance cost
To permanently replace all physical RAM
questions.correctAnswer: To extend virtual-memory backing when RAM pressure occurs, at a performance cost
questions.explanation:
Swap provides disk-backed space used by the memory manager.

Why: It can help under memory pressure, although disk access is slower than RAM.

Example: swapon --show reports active swap devices/files.

Student note: Swap is not a replacement for enough RAM for a busy workload.

study.title: swap
study.simple: Swap provides disk-backed space used by the memory manager.
steps: It can help under memory pressure, although disk access is slower than RAM.
study.example: swapon --show reports active swap devices/files.
study.pitfall: Swap is not a replacement for enough RAM for a busy workload.
study.remember: It can help under memory pressure, although disk access is slower than RAM.

keyTerms.meaning: Swap provides disk-backed space used by the memory manager.

questions.text: A regular file is created with base mode 666 and umask 027. What permission mode normally results?
questions.explanation:
umask removes selected permission bits from the requested new file mode.

Why: 666 masked with 027 produces 640.

Example: The owner can read/write, the group can read, and others have no permissions.

Student note: For a new directory, 777 masked with 027 produces 750.

study.remember: 666 masked with 027 produces 640.

questions.text: Which command safely adds an existing account to a supplementary group without replacing its other supplementary groups?
questions.explanation:
The -a append option with -G adds supplementary group membership.

Why: Without -a, -G can replace the account's existing supplementary groups.

Example: sudo usermod -aG developers learner can add a learner to developers.

Student note: A user may need a new login session to use the new membership.

study.remember: Without -a, -G can replace the account's existing supplementary groups.

keyTerms.meaning: The -a append option with -G adds supplementary group membership.

questions.text: A Linux server reports 'No space left on device'. Explain a careful diagnosis that distinguishes filesystem capacity, inode exhaustion and large directory usage.
questions.correctAnswer: Check df -h for full mounted filesystems, df -i for exhausted inodes, and du -sh or du -x on appropriate directories to locate storage usage. Check logs and mounts, identify safe cleanup or capacity expansion, preserve critical data, and verify after changes.
aiRubric: Uses safe cleanup/expansion and verifies result
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A write can fail when either data blocks or available inodes run out. Find the affected filesystem with df -h. Check inode availability using df -i. Locate large or excessive files safely, clean up or resize, then recheck. A flood of tiny cache files may exhaust inodes even when block space is available. Never start with indiscriminate rm -rf on a production server.
questions.explanation:
A write can fail when either data blocks or available inodes run out.

Method:
1. Find the affected filesystem with df -h.
2. Check inode availability using df -i.
3. Locate large or excessive files safely, clean up or resize, then recheck.

Example: A flood of tiny cache files may exhaust inodes even when block space is available.

Student note: Never start with indiscriminate rm -rf on a production server.

questions.text: A new staff member needs permission to use shared project files but should not receive administrator rights. Describe a suitable Linux account and group approach.
questions.correctAnswer: Create or verify the account, create or use a project group, add the user as a supplementary member with usermod -aG, set appropriate group ownership and access permissions on the shared directory, consider setgid/ACL if needed, test access, and avoid adding the user to sudo/wheel unnecessarily.
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Groups let several accounts share access without granting full administrator rights. Decide what the account needs to read, write or execute. Add it to the appropriate group without dropping other memberships. Set shared-directory ownership/modes and test as the real user. A team folder owned by group editors can be configured with group write and setgid. Membership changes can require a fresh login; sudo is not needed for routine shared-data access.

questions.text: A service suddenly uses nearly all CPU. Outline a diagnostic process before stopping or restarting it.
questions.correctAnswer: Use top/ps to identify PID, command and user; inspect service status and relevant logs (for example journalctl); determine whether heavy work is expected; consider nice/resource controls or correcting the cause; request clean termination/restart only if justified; measure again.
aiRubric: Identifies process with ps/top and PID
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A process can be busy without being broken; inspect evidence before disrupting service. Identify exactly which process consumes CPU. questions.text: Explain a practical approach for adding Linux swap space on a machine, including verification and making it persistent.
questions.correctAnswer: Check existing RAM and swap with free -h and swapon --show; ensure adequate disk space; create an appropriately sized swap file securely or use a swap partition; set safe file permissions (often 600 for a swap file); run mkswap and swapon; verify; add a suitable /etc/fstab entry for persistence and test.
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Swap is disk-backed virtual-memory capacity that can support a machine during RAM pressure. Inspect current active swap and storage. Prepare and activate a correctly secured swap area. Verify with swapon --show and configure persistence where needed. A swap file can be made active with mkswap and swapon once safely prepared. The exact file-creation procedure depends on filesystem capabilities; do not overwrite live data.
